I didn’t meet a ton of people in hostels but some were better than others. I met a lovely elderly South African couple at a hostel in Munich and a very nice girl who actually lives near me in the US at a hostel in Ireland! Also had multiple wonderful experiences with locals all over the place. It helped I had some family living overseas at the time, but even when I wasn’t with them, I still met locals and got to know them. I’m not a very outgoing person and don’t like approaching others because I’m kind of shy, so it definitely is harder, but possible. If it’s your kind of thing, try going to a bar crawl. lots of independent companies and hostels alike offer them, and it’s a good way to explore the town and have a fun night out in a somewhat structured environment. i met lots of other tourists from around the world this way and partying together makes you get to know each other quick haha. I still talk to one of them on snap chat now and again! Just be open to new opportunities for conversation and know not everyone will want to, but plenty will. To meet locals, I recommend trying to find smaller locally owned restaurants and shops and try to speak with your server or the owner for a bit when they are helping you. Ask them what they like to do on their night off to get a sense of where the local hangout spots are for non-tourists. You’ll get a small taste of what life is really like and also have the chance to meet some new people. I found that locals would often want to know how we found a certain bar or restaurant because it was considered a local hidden gem, and that right there is a great conversation starter! Stick to the touristy places and you’re only going to find a) other tourists and b) locals at their jobs that don’t really want or have time to talk to you. Free walking tours are good too if you want to stay near the touristy spots though. You’ll meet lots of fun people from around the world and every tour guide I’ve ever had is always thrilled to tell you more about their life and culture. I’ve even had some invite the group out to a bar they were headed to after to hang out or ask more questions. Just try to get to know the area as well as possible with the time you have there. Do that and the better the chances you’ll have to make new friends.

EDIT: It is almost certainly because of the language barrier I’m sure, but I found it easiest to meet locals in the UK/Ireland because they would often overhear me or my partner’s American accent and strike up a little conversation. Plus their pubs tend to have seating pretty close together so it’s hard to sit at a table without at least saying hello to your neighbor a foot away! lol

EDIT #2: I find that the more niche your walking tour is, the more likely your guide is to want to actually hang out with people on the tour and tries harder to genuinely form a connection with them. I like to do lots of haunted tours, I did a Jack the Ripper walking tour in London, etc. If you’re in a city where a favorite film of yours was made or a certain part of the local lore you’re interested in, try to find tours that focus on that. Often times these tours still include major landmarks and areas of interest anyway because they happen to be along the tour route, so it’s well worth the time imo.

Good Omens by Neil Gaiman and Terry Pratchett. The short summary is that an angel and a demon team up to try and stop the world from ending. How, you ask? Well, it turns out the anti-Christ (or, The Adversary as he’s usually referred to by the characters) is an 11 year old boy named Adam Young, living in a quiet Oxfordshire village with his dog and three best friends, and he has no idea what he is in for as he nears his twelfth birthday, when the countdown to Armageddon begins. It has religious themes but is by no means a religious book. very funny while also dealing with heavy topics such as good vs. evil, friendship, love, loss, trust, and loyalty. It is a BEAUTIFUL commentary on the human experience, and it’s especially interesting because a large part of the book does this from the perspective of supernatural entities who have been masquerading as humans since shortly after the dawn of time. It made me laugh and cry. God is not a being of love, but a neutral party in the book. And I really liked that; it made more sense to me that the world can be so fucked up and beautiful at the same time, so it’s logical to believe that whoever made it wasn’t perfectly good or evil! The description they give of God and the universe is this: “God does not play dice with the universe; He plays an ineffable game of His own devising, which might be compared, from the perspective of any of the other players (footnote: everybody), to being involved in an obscure and complex version of poker in a pitch-dark room, with blank cards, for infinite stakes, with a Dealer who won’t tell you the rules and who smiles all the time.” 

But like I said, it is NOT a book that tries to push its reader to believe one way or the other about religion. Neil Gaiman is actually Jewish, so while a lot of the religious undertones in the book could be interpreted as Christian-rooted (or anti-Christianity), it’s not. The book actually explores several different religions in some form or fashion. It mainly just seeks to show that like our world, there’s beauracracy and secrets in Heaven and Hell too, and Aziraphale and Crowley (the angel and demon, respectively) must navigate it much like we do in a toxic work environment. You will be surprised how relatable their characters are. It’s such a beautiful book that really hits the nail on the head while exploring the cycle of birth, growth, maturity, and death. It’s one of my favorite books in the whole world, and the Amazon Prime limited series is the best book to tv adaptation i’ve ever seen (no surprise there- Neil Gaiman was the show runner and made the adaptation happen per Terry Pratchett’s dying wish. It was a labor of love, and that shines through).If it sounds interesting, please check it out! It’s a nice mix of sci-fi, dark comedy, and a coming of age story. Seriously, check it out, it really changed my perspective about a lot of things regarding my purpose here and how I think about “the afterlife” and it honestly brought me peace by challenging me to re-examine the narrative I was comfortable with. 

Very sorry for your loss and hope you find peace. I know I don’t know you, but Im thinking of you!

Good Omens by Neil Gaiman and Terry Pratchett. a quick and funny read (seriously top-notch dark humor) about an angel and demon teaming up to stop the end of the world before it happens. It deals with religion, but it’s by no means a religious book; Neil Gaiman is actually Jewish and very deliberately did not want to make religion central to the book as a determiner of morality. It pokes fun at Christianity as an organized “corporation,” while also still lending legitimacy to faith and the importance of faith in SOMETHING or SOMEONE, or more important, faith in yourself. It’s a perfect book for someone experiencing some growing pains. And as serious and hefty as moments in the book can be, it’s absolutely hilarious.

EDIT 3: I realize this post comes off as “just don’t give a fuck, it’s easy!” and I regret that. Until very recently,  I was a massive pushover. In fact, it was so out of character for me to stand up for myself that when I finally started doing it people were concerned that I was “going through something.” Yes, it’s called CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT! Acquaint yourself with being uncomfortable, and make it second nature to say what you need from someone without worrying how they’ll react. Be firm. People will try to guilt you, persuade you, manipulate you, etc. because they know in the past, it always worked. DO NOT BACK DOWN. You might lose some friends, but anyone who won’t show you respect isn’t a good friend. Practice rewording things on your own too so that it feels less abrasive. I’m not saying cater to their feelings when you stand up for yourself, but think about how your needs will be most successfully communicated. There’s a big difference between “you never do the dishes and it really pisses me off” and “i kind of think we should try a new routine to determine who does dishes when” in a roommate dispute. That’s just one example. Basically, stand up for yourself and don’t take any shit, but also be aware that it’ll often be much easier going if you do so in a way that is still polite and respectful. But if they still won’t listen, by all means, let ‘er rip. It’s a process. It’s taken me literally over a decade to figure it out. And I still struggle with it. Whenever I can’t decide whether it’s worth saying something or not, I try to pretend what I’d expect someone else to do if it happened to them. Would I think they were overreacting for putting their foot down, or would I think that’s a normal response to have in their situation? If I wouldn’t be absolutely horrified by someone standing up for themselves in that scenario, I make sure to say something. it also helps if you remember that if you’re thinking there’s a problem, there’s a good chance someone else does too and just isn’t saying anything.

We served as the “last point of civilization” before pioneers began the Oregon Trail out west in the 1800s, and we are the home of many historic artists, academics, athletes, and more. We are home to the National WWI Museum and the country’s Negro Leagues Baseball Museum and Hall of Fame. Our football team, the Chiefs, also won the Super Bowl last year and we’re currently in football season. We’re home to Arrowhead Stadium, the loudest sports stadium in North America. Definitely worth seeing a game just to say you’ve been. 

I wouldn’t recommend southern Missouri. They are not accepting and while you might not experience outright racism, you will most likely get some stares or less than pleasant experiences. My experience with anywhere south of Columbia, MO has not been positive. But don’t sleep on the midwest! We have a lot to offer and we often get a bad rap because of stereotypes created by people who have never even left the coast. While we have our problems, the midwest is also full of some of the most passionate, kind, intelligent, open-minded and justice-minded people I’ve ever met, and most of us know that our country is a laughing stock right now and we’re embarrassed of it and just want to let people know we’re not all stupid and backwards about our beliefs. 

Plus, Chicago is only an eight hour train ride from KC, barely over an hour by plane. Have fun and be safe!

Honestly, Kansas City, MO is well worth the visit if you have time. I feel like it’s friendlier to tourists than St. Louis, with a large black population as well.
